body.working_title: Which forecasts do error measures rank first, and how long must the test set be?

body.text: When candidate point forecasts are fixed before any test data are seen, which candidate does each error measure (RMSE, MAE, MAPE, sMAPE) rank first, and how often does a test set of a given size rank the candidates in that same order?

body.definition: Root mean squared error of a point forecast f over a test set of outcomes y_1..y_n: sqrt(mean((y_t - f)^2)).
Mean absolute error of a point forecast f over a test set: mean(|y_t - f|).

Mean absolute percentage error of a point forecast f over a test set: 100 mean(|y_t - f| / |y_t|) over the outcomes that are not zero (outcomes equal to zero are left out, since the ratio is undefined).
Symmetric mean absolute percentage error of a point forecast f over a test set: 200 mean(|y_t - f| / (|y_t| + |f|)), where a pair with y_t = f (including y_t = f = 0) contributes 0.

A point forecast whose value is fixed before any test set is drawn and is the same for every test set. In this study each candidate is computed from the true outcome distribution (its mean, its median, the value with the lowest expected MAPE, the value with the lowest expected sMAPE, or zero); it is never estimated from a test set or from any other sample.

The value a measure gives a candidate forecast in the limit of an infinitely long test set from the outcome distribution: for RMSE sqrt(E[(Y - f)^2]); for MAE E|Y - f|; for MAPE 100 E[|Y - f| / |Y| given Y != 0]; for sMAPE 200 E[|Y - f| / (|Y| + |f|)]. Computed from the distribution itself (by numerical integration, or exact sums for counts), not from simulated test sets.
Of the candidate forecasts for one outcome distribution, the one with the lowest expected score under a given measure. It says which candidate the measure rewards, independently of any test set.

For one outcome distribution, one measure, one pair of candidate forecasts with different expected scores and one test-set size n: the probability that, in a test set of n outcomes drawn from the distribution, the measure gives the lower score to the candidate with the lower expected score. Ties count as disagreement. It is a property of how the measure compares two fixed forecasts on finite test sets; it is not about the value of the measure itself, nor about any forecast estimated from data.

body.text: Scope, agreed with the supervisor (AC2) on 2026-11-15, before any design or run. What this study does: it fixes candidate point forecasts in advance from the true outcome distribution, scores them with RMSE, MAE, MAPE and sMAPE, and reports (1) which candidate each measure ranks first by its expected score, computed from the distribution (what the measure rewards), and (2) per test-set size, how often a finite test set ranks a pair of candidates in the same order as their expected scores (ranking agreement), as estimates with 99% intervals, not as tests against a threshold. What this study does not do: it estimates no forecast from data, so it says nothing about the forecast that minimises a measure on a sample (for RMSE the sample mean, for MAE the sample median) or about how well such a forecast estimates the mean or the median (its bias, efficiency or consistency); and it does not study a measure's value as an estimator of its expected score (its bias or variance across test sets). The only finite-sample quantity is ranking agreement: whether a test set orders two fixed forecasts as their expected scores do.

The supervisor (AC2), 2026-11-15: no statistical test (such as Friedman with Nemenyi) between candidate forecasts. In a simulation the number of test sets is chosen by us, so a test's verdict would reflect that number rather than the measures. Instead, count how many times each candidate is chosen by each measure, plot the distribution of the chosen candidates, and use its mean as the central tendency. The supervisor's words: "we don't need a proper statistical test here. Just count how many times each functional was chosen. Plot distributions and use their mean to get the central tendency."

The supervisor (AC2), 2026-11-15: no forecasting model (ETS(A,N,N) is dropped): outcomes are generated directly from known distributions, and the candidates are their quantiles at levels 0.01 to 0.99, their mean, and the values that minimise each measure's expected score, computed by whatever works (closed forms, or one very large reference sample). The supervisor's words: "We need to generate quantile and mean and which minimise what"; "Whatever works to get quantiles. We don't need to forecast actually".

The supervisor (AC2), 2026-11-15: continuous outcomes are positive. Normal and Laplace outcomes are placed at a level high enough relative to their spread that values at or below zero do not occur in practice; outcomes with outliers are included; counts are included, with sMAPE computed on them (a correct zero forecast scores 0) and MAPE not computed, since one zero outcome makes it infinite. The supervisor's words: "For normal and Laplace, use very high level to avoid zeroes. Don't forget outliers. Use counts. mape is inf, smape can be counted."

body.definition: Mean absolute percentage error of a point forecast f over a test set: 100 mean(|y_t - f| / |y_t|). It is computed only on continuous positive outcomes; on counts it is not computed, since a single zero outcome makes it infinite.

For one outcome distribution, one measure and one test-set size n: for each candidate forecast, the share of simulated test sets of n outcomes in which the measure gives that candidate the lowest score among all candidates (a tie between k candidates gives each 1/k). Its distribution over the candidates, and that distribution's mean, show where a test set of n outcomes puts the measure's choice. It is a count over test sets of a choice among fixed forecasts; it is not a test, and it is not about the value of the measure itself nor about any forecast estimated from data.

body.text: Scope, agreed with the supervisor (AC2) on 2026-11-15, before any design or run (restated after DC1 to DC3). What this study does: it fixes candidate point forecasts in advance from the true outcome distribution (its quantiles at levels 0.01 to 0.99, its mean, and the values that minimise each measure's expected score), scores them with RMSE, MAE, MAPE and sMAPE, and reports (1) which candidate each measure ranks first by its expected score, computed from the distribution (what the measure rewards), and (2) per test-set size, how often each candidate is ranked first in simulated test sets (selection shares), with the mean of the chosen candidates as their central tendency, as estimates with 99% intervals, not as tests. What this study does not do: it estimates no forecast from data, so it says nothing about the forecast that minimises a measure on a sample (for RMSE the sample mean, for MAE the sample median) or about how well such a forecast estimates the mean or the median (its bias, efficiency or consistency); it fits no forecasting model; and it does not study a measure's value as an estimator of its expected score (its bias or variance across test sets). Its only finite-sample quantity is which of the fixed candidates a test set of n outcomes ranks first.

The supervisor (AC2), 2026-11-15: no statistical test (such as Friedman with Nemenyi) between candidate forecasts. In a simulation the number of test sets is chosen by us, so a test's verdict would reflect that number rather than the measures. Instead, count how many times each candidate is chosen by each measure, plot the distribution of the chosen candidates, and use its mean as the central tendency. The supervisor's words, verbatim: "You are right, we don't need a proper statistical test here. Just count how many times each functional was chosen. Plot distributions and use their mean to get the vengeance tendency." ("vengeance" stands for "central").

body.definition: Outcomes from a normal distribution with mean 100 and standard deviation 5, and from a Laplace distribution with location 100 and standard deviation 5 (scale 5 / sqrt(2)). Twenty standard deviations above zero, so that outcomes at or below zero do not occur in practice; mean and median are both 100.

Outcomes y = 100 exp(x): lognormal (x normal with mean 0 and standard deviation s, s = 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1) and log-Laplace (x Laplace with location 0 and scale b, b = 0.25, 0.5); and gamma outcomes with mean 100 and shape 2, 5 or 20. All are positive with a density that vanishes at zero, so the expected MAPE is finite.
Symmetric outliers: 95% of outcomes from N(100, 5^2) and 5% from N(100, 15^2). Upward spikes: outcomes from N(100, 5^2), of which 5% are multiplied by 3, as from promotions.
